title: Introduction to the Letter to Titus
subtitle: A concise guide to the authorship, setting, people, opponents, and enduring message of Paul’s letter to the coworker he left on Crete to set the young churches in order.

blocks.text: The letter opens in the name of Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, and its greeting is among the fullest in his collection. Before it names the recipient it sets out the purpose of his commission: Paul serves the faith of God’s elect, their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, and their hope of eternal life, promised before the ages began by the God who cannot lie. The writer speaks with apostolic authority, counts himself among those who were once foolish and disobedient, and settles his travel plans and winter quarters like a man whose movements are his own.

The early church received Titus as Paul’s without hesitation. Its phrases echo in Christian writing near the turn of the second century, Irenaeus and others cite it by name before A.D. 200, and it stands among Paul’s letters in the earliest surviving lists of New Testament writings. Its teaching on grace, justification, the Spirit, and the hope of Christ’s appearing was treated as apostolic from the start, and congregations shaped their practice of appointing elders partly by its instructions. The ancient churches knew the difference between Paul’s letters and pious imitations, and they placed this one firmly among the former.

Modern doubts usually rest on four observations: the vocabulary, the church order, the character of the error, and the travels the letter assumes. Titus shares many rare words with 1 and 2 Timothy, and some readers conclude that a later disciple composed all three. Yet a three-chapter letter about appointing elders and correcting household conduct will naturally draw on words absent from letters about the law or the resurrection, and the body of text is far too small for word counts to settle the question of authorship. Paul also wrote through secretaries, and a change of scribe or of subject can account for a change of style.

The church order of Titus is simple rather than advanced. Paul appointed elders in the churches of Galatia on his first journey, and here Titus does the same in the towns of Crete. The titles elder and overseer describe one office (1:5, 7), with no sign of a single bishop presiding over a region, which is what one would expect in the apostolic generation and not in the second century. The false teaching, with its Jewish myths, purity rules, and quarrels about the law, resembles the trouble Paul had already confronted in Galatia and Colossae far more than the elaborate systems of later times.

The doctrine of the letter carries Paul’s fingerprints. God saves by His own mercy, apart from works of righteousness that we have done (3:5); believers are justified by His grace and made heirs in hope of eternal life (3:7); the Spirit is poured out richly through Jesus Christ (3:6). Grace produces a life of good works without those works becoming its ground, the same balance Paul strikes in Ephesians 2:8–10. The personal details, including the names Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos and the plan to winter at Nicopolis, are the sort of incidental remarks a forger had little reason to invent and good reason to avoid.

Titus cannot be fitted into the narrative of Acts. Paul passed the southern coast of Crete only once in that account, as a prisoner on his way to Rome, sheltering briefly at Fair Havens before a gale drove the ship out to sea. There was no opportunity on that voyage to plant churches across the island or to leave a coworker behind, and Acts mentions no winter at Nicopolis. The letter assumes a ministry on Crete that Luke never describes, and the most natural explanation is that it took place after the events with which Acts closes.

Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome for two full years, preaching without hindrance, and it records no verdict and no execution. In the letters written during that confinement Paul expected release and planned fresh visits, and early Christian memory spoke of a season of renewed labor before a second arrest and death under Nero. If Paul was freed about A.D. 62, a mission on Crete with Titus, a departure while the work remained unfinished, and the sending of this letter all fit well into the years that followed. A date of about A.D. 63 to 65 places Titus close to 1 Timothy and before the final imprisonment reflected in 2 Timothy.

The letter does not name the place where it was written. Paul says he has decided to spend the winter at Nicopolis, so he had not yet arrived there. Several cities bore that name, which means city of victory, but the likeliest is Nicopolis in Epirus, a Roman foundation on the western coast of Greece built to celebrate Augustus’s triumph at Actium. It made a natural base for work further north toward Dalmatia. Paul may have written from Macedonia, from Corinth, or from some stop on the road through Greece, and Zenas the lawyer and Apollos appear to have carried the letter to Crete.

The timing helps explain the letter’s brevity and its businesslike tone. Paul is still free, still traveling, and still directing a team of coworkers. He intends to send Artemas or Tychicus to relieve Titus, and once the replacement arrives Titus is to make every effort to reach Nicopolis before winter closes the sea lanes. There is no mention of chains, trials, or approaching death, as there is in 2 Timothy. The letter reads as an apostle’s working commission, written in the middle of active ministry and intended to be read aloud in the churches as the warrant for Titus’s task.

Crete is the largest island of the Aegean world and one of the largest in the Mediterranean, stretching about 160 miles from west to east and varying from roughly 8 to 35 miles in width. A spine of mountains runs its length, rising above 8,000 feet at Mount Ida, with fertile plains and sheltered valleys between the ranges. The northern coast faces the Aegean and the Greek mainland, while the southern coast looks across open water toward Africa. Lying astride the sea routes linking Greece, Asia, Egypt, and Italy, the island was a natural meeting point for sailors, merchants, and travelers.

Long before the classical age, Crete was home to a brilliant Bronze Age civilization centered on great palace complexes such as Knossos. Later the island was divided among dozens of independent Greek city-states, and ancient poetry already called it a land of a hundred cities. Those towns were often at odds with one another, and Cretans became known as mercenary soldiers, archers for hire, and in some periods pirates. Rome subdued the island in 67 B.C. after a hard campaign and joined it with Cyrene on the north African coast into one province, governed from Gortyn in the broad southern plain of the Mesara.

Crete also carried a reputation that Paul acknowledges frankly. He cites one of their own prophets, an early Cretan poet, who described his countrymen as always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons, and Paul adds that the testimony is true (1:12–13). Greek speech even coined a verb from the island’s name meaning to lie or to cheat. One notorious provocation was the Cretan claim to possess the tomb of Zeus, which other Greeks regarded as a slander against an immortal god. Paul is being realistic about the culture, and he never implies that Cretans lie beyond the reach of grace. The gospel had to reshape a society where deceit, greed, and appetite had become proverbial.

A substantial Jewish population lived on the island. A Roman letter from the second century B.C. on behalf of the Jews was addressed in part to Gortyn, and Jewish writers of the first century list Crete among the lands where their people had settled. Cretans were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost and heard the apostles declare the mighty works of God in their own tongue (Acts 2:11). Some of them may have carried the message home long before Paul arrived. That Jewish presence also helps explain the shape of the false teaching, which drew on Jewish legends and on rules about ritual purity.

The only scene set on Crete in Acts comes from Paul’s voyage to Rome (Acts 27:7–21). The ship crept along the southern shore past Cape Salmone and anchored at Fair Havens near the town of Lasea. Paul warned that pressing on would bring loss of cargo and life, but the centurion trusted the pilot and the owner, and the crew tried to reach the harbor of Phoenix to winter there. A violent northeasterly wind then drove them helplessly out to sea. Paul later reminded the sailors that they should have listened and stayed at Crete. Some years afterward he returned to the island as a free man and as a preacher.

sections.title: Titus in the Story of Paul

blocks.text: Titus is never named in Acts, yet Paul’s letters show him to be one of the apostle’s most trusted partners. He was a Greek, probably converted through Paul himself, for Paul calls him his true son in the faith they shared (1:4). When Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem to lay before the leaders of the church the gospel they preached among the Gentiles, they took Titus with them, and he became a living test case. False brothers pressed the point, yet he was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1–5). His very presence confirmed that Gentiles enter the people of God by faith in Christ.

During Paul’s long stay at Ephesus, Titus became the apostle’s envoy to Corinth. He seems to have carried a severe letter to that troubled church, and Paul waited for his return with such anxiety that he could find no rest at Troas when Titus failed to appear. When at last they met in Macedonia, Titus brought word of the Corinthians’ grief, zeal, and repentance, and Paul was comforted by his coming (2 Corinthians 7:5–16). Titus then went back to Corinth to complete the collection for the poor saints of Judea, and Paul commended him as his partner and fellow worker (2 Corinthians 8:16–24).

blocks.title: Titus Through the Years
blocks.note: Dates are approximate. Acts never names Titus, so his story is pieced together from incidental remarks in Paul’s letters.

events.title: A Greek Convert
events.description: Titus comes to faith, apparently through Paul’s own ministry, and joins the circle of workers based at Antioch.

events.title: Uncircumcised at Jerusalem
events.description: Paul takes Titus to Jerusalem, where the church leaders do not compel him to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1–3).

events.title: Envoy to Corinth
events.description: From Ephesus Paul sends Titus to Corinth during the most painful stage of that church’s rebellion against his authority.

events.title: Good News in Macedonia
events.description: Titus meets Paul with word of Corinthian repentance, then returns to complete the collection for Judea (2 Corinthians 7–8).

events.title: Left on Crete
events.description: After ministering together on the island, Paul leaves Titus to set the churches in order and appoint elders in every town.

events.title: Summoned to Nicopolis
events.description: Paul sends this letter and asks Titus to join him for the winter once Artemas or Tychicus arrives to replace him.

events.title: Gone to Dalmatia
events.description: During Paul’s final imprisonment Titus is away serving in Dalmatia, on the eastern shore of the Adriatic (2 Timothy 4:10).

blocks.text: The portrait that emerges is of a coworker who stayed steady under pressure, handled difficult congregations wisely, and could be trusted with money and conflict alike. That is why he was left on Crete. Paul had no intention of sending a novice to the island; he left a seasoned man who had already seen a church through division, defiance, and reconciliation. The last glimpse of Titus in Scripture comes in Paul’s final letter, which says he had gone to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10). Later Christian tradition remembered him returning to Crete and serving the churches there into old age.

Paul says he left Titus on Crete to set in order the things that were lacking and to appoint elders in every city (1:5). The words imply that the gospel had taken root in several towns, that congregations already existed, and that their organization was unfinished. These were young churches. They had believers but no recognized leaders, converts but no settled pattern of teaching, and households still learning what the faith required of them at home and in public. Paul had apparently stayed only a short time, and Titus was to complete what the apostle had begun.

The congregations met in homes, as churches across the Roman world did. The household was the basic unit of ancient society, gathering grandparents, married couples, children, unmarried young men, and slaves under one roof and within one economy. That is why the letter speaks so directly to older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and slaves (2:1–10), and why an elder must have faithful children and a well-ordered home (1:6). An elder’s household served as a small preview of the church he would lead, and the false teachers were doing their damage precisely by overturning whole houses (1:11).

The churches also lived under the eye of wary neighbors and Roman officials. A new religious movement that made wives defiant, slaves insolent, or citizens unruly could expect hostility, and outsiders would judge the gospel by the behavior of its followers. Paul repeatedly frames his household instructions with that audience in view: that the word of God be not blasphemed, that opponents be ashamed with nothing evil to say, and that believers adorn the teaching of God our Savior in all things (2:5, 8, 10). He then asks them to be subject to rulers, ready for every good work, and gentle toward everyone (3:1–2).

Many of the converts had come out of the very habits for which their island was known, and Paul makes no attempt to hide it. He includes himself among those who were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, enslaved to passions and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another (3:3). The Cretan churches were communities of people rescued from that life by the kindness and love of God, and their changed conduct was the plainest evidence that the message they believed was true. The pastoral program of the whole letter is to make that change visible in every home and town.

Paul describes the opponents in sharp terms. There were many unruly men, idle talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party (1:10). They were teaching things they ought not to teach, for the sake of shameful gain, and they were upsetting entire households. Their mouths had to be stopped. The language points to insiders, or at least to men claiming a place within the congregations, who were exploiting the absence of established leaders to win a following and an income. Ancient travelers who taught for pay were common, and the young churches were easy targets.

Their teaching had a Jewish flavor. Paul warns against Jewish fables and the commandments of men who turn from the truth (1:14), and later against foolish questions, genealogies, strife, and quarrels about the law, which he calls unprofitable and vain (3:9). The teachers seem to have spun speculative stories around biblical family lines and to have insisted on purity rules that went beyond anything God had given. The trouble lay in human additions and in an emphasis on outward ritual that left the heart unchanged. Paul elsewhere calls the law itself holy, just, and good, and nothing in Titus sets him against the Scriptures of Israel.

Paul answers their purity rules with a principle: to the pure all things are pure, while to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, because even their mind and conscience are defiled (1:15). The statement concerns the human regulations he has just named and leaves untouched the distinctions God Himself established. Purity begins in a heart cleansed by faith, and no ritual can supply what an unclean conscience lacks. The teachers’ preoccupation with external rules masked inner corruption, and their conduct exposed it to anyone who cared to look.

The final test was conduct. They profess to know God, Paul writes, yet by their works they deny Him, being detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work (1:16). That verdict stands in deliberate contrast to the rest of the letter, where true believers are to be ready for every good work and zealous for good works. The false teachers talked much and produced nothing good. Titus is to rebuke them sharply so that they may become sound in the faith, and if a divisive man persists after a first and second warning, he is to be refused as one who stands self-condemned (3:10–11).

The immediate reason was practical. Titus needed a written commission. Paul had given him instructions in person when he left him on Crete, but a letter from the apostle, read aloud in the congregations, would confirm his authority to appoint elders and to silence the troublemakers. That is why Paul can close the second chapter by telling Titus to speak, exhort, and rebuke with all authority, and to let no one disregard him (2:15). The letter is addressed to one man, yet its final blessing, grace be with you all, shows that the churches were meant to hear every word.

The second reason was protective. Elders were needed because false teachers were filling the vacuum. The qualifications Paul lists in 1:6–9 dwell on character far more than on gifts: a blameless reputation, a faithful family, self-control, hospitality, love of what is good, justice, holiness, and a firm grip on the trustworthy word. An elder must be able both to encourage others by sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it. Leaders of tested character would become the churches’ chief defense once Titus moved on to Nicopolis and beyond.

The deepest purpose was theological. Paul wanted the Cretan believers to see that sound doctrine and good works belong together. The letter contains two of the richest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament. The first declares that the saving grace of God has appeared to all people and trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, living sober, upright, and godly lives in this present age while we wait for the blessed hope, the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:11–13). That appearing is the visible, personal return of the Lord in glory, the hope that shapes how believers live while they wait.

The second summary celebrates the moment when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared (3:4). He saved us apart from any righteous deeds of our own, by His mercy, through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit (3:5). Baptism signifies that washing, while the new birth itself is the Spirit’s work in a believing heart. Paul draws the practical conclusion at once: those who have believed God must be careful to devote themselves to good works (3:8). Salvation is a free gift, and its fruit is a life that meets real needs and commends the gospel to others.

The letter also served the wider mission. Paul asks Titus to help Zenas and Apollos on their way and urges the believers to learn to maintain good works for pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful (3:13–14). Even the closing lines reveal a network of workers moving across the Mediterranean, sustained by the churches they served. Crete was to become more than a mission field. Its congregations were to grow into a base that welcomed, supported, and sent others, and their generosity toward traveling workers was itself one of the good works the letter commends.

Titus is brief, but it is carefully built. Chapter 1 lays the foundation, stating Paul’s apostolic purpose, setting out the qualifications of elders, and drawing a portrait of the false teachers. Chapter 2 moves into the household, showing each group how to live in a way that befits sound doctrine, and then grounds that teaching in the grace that has appeared and the glory that is yet to appear. Chapter 3 widens the view to public life, recalls the mercy that saved the believers, and closes with warnings, travel plans, and greetings.

Several key words run through all three chapters. God and Christ are both called Savior, a title that appears six times in this short letter. Good works are mentioned again and again, and the word sound, meaning healthy, describes the teaching, faith, and speech that Titus is to promote. Truth stands against myth, godliness against empty profession, and hope against the passions of the present age. Titus shares much with 1 Timothy, yet the two letters address quite different situations, as the comparison below shows.

blocks.title: Titus at a Glance
rows: Author
The apostle Paul, writing as a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ
Recipient
Titus, a Greek coworker left on Crete, together with the congregations who would hear the letter read
Date
About A.D. 63–65, between Paul’s first and second Roman imprisonments
Place of writing
Not stated; probably Macedonia or Greece, on Paul’s route toward Nicopolis in Epirus
Setting
Young house churches in the towns of Crete, lacking elders and troubled by teachers of the circumcision party
Purpose
To confirm Titus’s authority, appoint qualified elders, silence false teachers, and show how grace produces good works
Structure
Leaders and opponents (chapter 1); conduct in the household (chapter 2); conduct in public life and closing instructions (chapter 3)
Key words
Savior, sound teaching, godliness, good works, grace, and the hope of eternal life
Key passages

blocks.title: Titus and 1 Timothy Compared
rows: Church situation
Young congregations on Crete with no settled leadership yet
An established church at Ephesus with elders already serving
Leadership
Elders to be appointed in every town; deacons are not mentioned
Overseers and deacons described, with guidance for honoring and correcting elders
False teaching
Jewish fables, human purity rules, genealogies, and quarrels about the law, pursued for gain
Myths, endless genealogies, misuse of the law, and the forbidding of marriage and foods
Gospel summaries
Grace that has appeared and trains believers (2:11–14); mercy that saves and renews (3:4–7)
Christ came to save sinners (1:15); the one Mediator (2:5–6); the mystery of godliness (3:16)
The delegate
Titus, a seasoned Gentile troubleshooter on a temporary posting, soon to be relieved
Timothy, a younger and more reserved coworker urged to let no one despise his youth
